title: Fine-Tuning & Adaptation

character.name: The Sculptor
character.tagline: The model is the marble. I just chip it toward your masterpiece.

oneLiner: When and how to adapt a base model — and why prompting or RAG is often the smarter first move.
analogy: A base LLM is a wildly talented generalist actor. Prompting is handing them a script for tonight's scene. RAG is giving them cue cards with the latest facts. Fine-tuning is sending them to months of method-acting school so they permanently nail a specific accent or character. School is powerful but expensive, and it doesn't teach them today's news — for facts you still want cue cards (RAG). The pro move: try prompting first, add RAG for knowledge, and fine-tune only when you need consistent style, format, or specialized behavior at scale.
objectives: Understand fine-tuning as updating a model's weights on task-specific examples.
Compare prompting vs RAG vs fine-tuning and when each fits.
Know parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA/PEFT) and why it's popular.
Recognize the data, cost, and maintenance implications of fine-tuning.
keyConcepts: Fine-tuning continues training a base model on curated examples to specialize its behavior, style, or format.
It's best for teaching consistent tone/format or narrow tasks — not for injecting frequently changing facts (use RAG for that).
The usual escalation: start with prompting, add RAG for knowledge, then fine-tune if you still need more consistency or specialization.
LoRA/PEFT (parameter-efficient fine-tuning) trains small adapter weights instead of the whole model, cutting cost and storage.
Fine-tuning needs quality labeled examples; poor data bakes in bad behavior.
Fine-tuned models require versioning and re-tuning as needs change — an ongoing maintenance cost.

keyTerms.plain: Extra training to specialize a model's behavior/style.
The big pretrained generalist you start from.
Cheap fine-tuning that trains tiny add-on weights, not the whole model.
A small trained module bolted onto a frozen base model.
When over-tuning makes a model lose skills it used to have.

scenarios.scenario: A team wants the model to ALWAYS respond in their brand's very specific voice and a fixed template, across millions of requests.
scenarios.question: Which approach is the best long-term fit?

options.label: Fine-tuning on many brand-voice examples to bake in the consistent style/format

scenarios.explanation: Consistent style/format at scale is a classic fine-tuning use case. RAG is for knowledge, not tone; prompting alone can drift across many requests.

scenarios.scenario: A startup wants to fine-tune a large model but has a limited GPU budget and storage.
scenarios.question: Which technique reduces the cost of fine-tuning?

options.label: LoRA/PEFT — train small adapter weights instead of the full model
Train the entire model from scratch

scenarios.explanation: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA/PEFT) updates a small number of adapter parameters, dramatically lowering compute and storage versus full fine-tuning.

quiz.question: Fine-tuning primarily involves:
options: Adding documents to the prompt at query time
Updating a model's weights by training on task-specific examples
quiz.answer: Updating a model's weights by training on task-specific examples
quiz.explanation: Fine-tuning continues training on curated data to specialize the model, changing its weights (unlike prompting or RAG).

quiz.question: For injecting frequently changing facts, you should generally use:
quiz.explanation: RAG supplies current facts at query time; fine-tuning bakes in behavior/style and is poorly suited to rapidly changing knowledge.

quiz.question: What is LoRA / PEFT?
options: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning that trains small adapter weights instead of the whole model
quiz.answer: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning that trains small adapter weights instead of the whole model
quiz.explanation: PEFT methods like LoRA train a small set of additional parameters, making fine-tuning far cheaper and lighter to store.

quiz.question: A sensible default escalation order for building with LLMs is:
options: Prompting → RAG → fine-tuning, escalating only as needed
quiz.answer: Prompting → RAG → fine-tuning, escalating only as needed
quiz.explanation: Start cheap and simple (prompting), add RAG for knowledge, and fine-tune only when consistency/specialization demands it.

quiz.question: A downside of fine-tuning to keep in mind is:
options: It requires quality data and ongoing maintenance/versioning
It instantly updates with world news
It removes the need for evaluation
quiz.answer: It requires quality data and ongoing maintenance/versioning
quiz.explanation: Fine-tuning needs good labeled examples and must be re-done as requirements change; poor data can bake in bad behavior.
